name: Emeka Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee lineworker on a city crew, so it's less climbing mountains and more digging up pavements on the east side. A lot of my day is underground cable, holding the lamp while Rosa, our cable jointer, makes the joint, then backfilling the trench and arguing with the traffic. Some days we're up poles in the old estates where the wires still run overhead. I like that I can drive past a street and know I helped keep its lights on.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay, mainly, for now. I'm on the trainee rate, Ama's still in her second year of nursing, and our flat on Kestrel Road costs more than half of what I take home. The other thing is the waiting, standing by a hole for two hours while somebody finds a permit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. Everybody at the depot was saying the robots were coming for the cable work, and here we are still holding lamps. I'd probably post a meme of Rosa's face when someone mentions AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine, maybe even good. I'd get my qualification on schedule and the pay jump that comes with it. The only thing I'd miss is the little bit of help I get from the chatbot when I'm studying cable ratings at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the training and keep my head in the books for the next assessment in March. Once I'm qualified, I'd start putting money aside, because right now I've got maybe two weeks of rent in the bank. I'd stay in the union and keep going to the youth section meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty relaxed. Normal life, just slightly easier paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use the chatbot for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly quizzing me before tests, like what size cable for what load, or explaining a diagram my tutor rushed through. I check it against the book, because it got a fuse rating wrong once. I'd never use it on site, that's Rosa's job and she's better than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If life carries on like this, what's the first thing you'd spend more money on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deposit on a slightly bigger place, so Ama has a desk for her studying instead of the ironing board. That's the dream for next year. Nothing fancy.

S0.say: He'd say he told everyone so, since the depot was sure robots were coming for cable work and they're all still holding lamps. He'd likely post a joke about his jointer Rosa's reaction to AI.
S0.think: It's fine or even good for him: qualification on schedule and the pay jump that follows. He'd only miss the small help a chatbot gives him studying cable ratings at night.
S0.do: Continues training and studies for the March assessment. Starts saving once qualified, since he has about two weeks of rent banked, and keeps attending union youth meetings.
S0.feel: Calm and relaxed, normal life with slightly easier paperwork.
S0.quote: I'd get my qualification on schedule and the pay jump that comes with it.
S0.fieldNote: He uses AI tools carefully and only for study, checking them against the book after catching an error. His calm comes from a clear path: qualify, get the pay rise, move to a bigger place so Ama can study. He has almost no savings but feels secure if nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it has to be done right, with the workers at the table. The network belongs to everyone, it should be run for people, not to make shareholders a few percent more. I'd say that at the union and I'd share it online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think city line work is safer than most jobs. You can't send a computer down a flooded trench full of old lead cable from the 1960s. But the planning side, the fault finding, the paperwork, that shrinks, and the new jobs might go to people better with computers than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get decent at whatever tools they bring in, once I'd seen them work on a couple of jobs. I'd ask the union to push for the training to be paid and in work hours. And I'd keep a closer eye on which teams are growing, because I've heard battery storage and car chargers are hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but okay. It's change I think I could handle if the company plays fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing Rosa use it and not swear at it, honestly. If the older ones on the crew say it saves a dig, I'm in. If they say it's rubbish, I'll leave it on the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The control room people who route the crews, because that's a computer job anyway. My friend Kwame works there, and he's already joking about dusting off his CV. Out on the street, we'd be fine for a while.

S1.say: Change has to be done right with workers at the table, because the network belongs to everyone and should be run for people rather than shareholders. He'd say it at the union and share it online.
S1.think: Urban line work is safer than most because no computer goes down a flooded trench of old cable, but planning, fault finding and paperwork could shrink. New jobs might go to people better with computers than him.
S1.do: Learns new tools once he's seen them work on a few jobs and asks the union to win paid training in work hours. Watches teams like battery storage and car chargers that are hiring.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy but okay, confident he could handle it if the company plays fair.
S1.quote: You can't send a computer down a flooded trench full of old lead cable from the 1960s.
S1.fieldNote: His trust in new tools runs through the older crew: if Rosa approves, he adopts it. He combines a public-ownership outlook with fairly relaxed personal judgement. His concern shifts to colleagues in the control room, like his friend Kwame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed, and the government needs to step in now, not after. I'd say the robots should belong to all of us if they're doing all of the work. I'd be at the protests with the nurses and the drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, two years is scary for someone with no savings. If robots can joint cable and dig trenches, I'm a trainee they don't need to finish training. Ama might be okay in nursing for longer, but she wouldn't be qualified yet either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut right back, no gym, no football tickets, cheaper phone plans, everything. I'd go to the union about what they're doing and join whatever action came. We'd probably move back to my mum's place in Linden Park for a while, which neither of us wants, and we'd put off any idea of getting a bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama, the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're a team, and if one of us is still working, we're fine. I'd tell her to finish her course whatever happens, because caring for people might be the last thing they hand to a machine. And I'd probably make her laugh by saying I'll be her stay-at-home husband.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years change whether you'd retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, because two years isn't enough time to finish anything. By the time I'd got a certificate in batteries or chargers, the robots would be doing that as well. So in this one I'd just hold on and fight for some kind of support.

S2.say: The government needs to step in now, and if robots do all the work they should belong to everyone. He'd join protests alongside nurses and drivers.
S2.think: Two years is frightening with no savings, since a trainee is easy to drop when robots can joint cable and dig. Ama wouldn't be qualified yet either.
S2.do: Cuts back on the gym, football tickets and phone plans, and joins any union action. Moves back to his mum's place in Linden Park for a while and shelves plans for a bigger flat.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake doing sums in his head.
S2.quote: I'd tell her to finish her course whatever happens, because caring for people might be the last thing they hand to a machine.
S2.fieldNote: In the fast scenario he sees retraining as pointless and switches to holding on and collective action. He leans on his relationship with Ama and on his mother's home as a safety net. He keeps a sense of humour even when alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and start planning who does what before it hits. I'd want every utility worker to have a retraining fund and a guarantee. I'd probably go on the union's local radio slot if they asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd be qualified and have a couple of years on proper pay. That gives me something to put by. But I'm not stupid, my job still goes in the end, so I'd need to be building the next thing while I do this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my training and then sign up for an evening course in substation and battery systems, maybe two nights a week. I'd try to save a few hundred a month once the pay goes up. And I'd keep pushing the union, because the deal you get early is the deal you live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. It's like a storm warning, you hate it but at least you can tie things down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why batteries and substations, if robots get those too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I think somebody still has to sign off on the big stuff for a while, a person who carries the blame if it blows. I might be wrong. It's a guess, not a plan, I'll admit that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for, those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the company starts sending a robot truck out with a crew to try it. And when Rosa gets that look that means she's worried. She's been doing this twenty-two years and she can smell trouble.

S3.say: There are five years to plan, so every utility worker should get a retraining fund and a guarantee. He'd speak on the union's local radio slot if asked.
S3.think: He'd qualify and get a couple of years on proper pay, giving him something to save. But his job still ends, so he'd need to build the next thing alongside it.
S3.do: Finishes his training, then takes an evening course in substation and battery systems two nights a week. Saves a few hundred a month once his pay rises and keeps pushing the union for an early deal.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, like a storm warning that gives you time to tie things down.
S3.quote: It's like a storm warning, you hate it but at least you can tie things down.
S3.fieldNote: Five years flips him from holding on to preparing, with a specific evening course in mind. He's honest that his choice of substations and batteries is a guess. He watches his senior colleague Rosa as an early warning system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. Make the companies pay into a fund, guarantee retraining, and keep the network public. I'd vote for whoever promised that, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, which is young enough to start again. I'd have a qualification, ten years of experience and hopefully a bit saved. I'd be more worried about Rosa than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get qualified and start using the planning software the engineers use, so I'm not just a pair of hands. Then I'd pick a course, maybe in grid control, and do it slowly. I'd save for the first time in my life, even if it's only a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than scared. It's far enough off that I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be more worried about Rosa. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's fifty-one, in ten years she's sixty-one and not ready to stop, but nobody's hiring a sixty-one-year-old to retrain. She taught me everything. If the deal doesn't look after people like her, it's not a fair deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with ten years than with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five I'd grab the first course going. With ten I'd look properly, maybe even ask Ama what hospitals need, like electrical engineers for their equipment. Time lets you choose instead of just run.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do this properly, so companies should pay into a fund, retraining should be guaranteed and the network kept public. He'd vote for whoever promised that.
S4.think: At thirty-seven he'd be young enough to start again, with a qualification, experience and some savings. He worries more for his senior colleague Rosa than for himself.
S4.do: Qualifies and learns the engineers' planning software in the first year, then takes a slow course, perhaps in grid control. Starts saving for the first time, even small amounts.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than scared.
S4.quote: Time lets you choose instead of just run.
S4.fieldNote: The longer runway makes him feel almost safe for himself and turns his concern to older colleagues like Rosa. He'd use the time to choose carefully, even thinking about hospital engineering through Ama. His politics shows in how he'd vote, not just in union talk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to finish anything, not my training and not Ama's. What would help is money that keeps people afloat while things settle, and somebody making sure trainees aren't the first ones dropped. And a promise that robots on a public network serve the public.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who've been doing this longest. Everyone talks about young people needing to adapt, but I can adapt. Rosa taught me how to make a joint that lasts forty years, and nobody's going to pay her for that knowledge.

headlineQuote: Rosa taught me how to make a joint that lasts forty years, and nobody's going to pay her for that knowledge.
portrait: Emeka Baker is a 27-year-old trainee on a city line crew, digging trenches and holding the lamp for cable jointer Rosa, while his partner Ama studies nursing and rent eats over half his pay. He uses AI tools a little for study, checks them against the book, and adopts new tools once the older crew trust them. He's calm if AI fizzles and only uneasy about steady change, but alarmed by AGI in two years, when he'd cut everything and move back to his mum's. With five or ten years he turns to retraining in substations, batteries or grid control. His politics favours public ownership and paid retraining, and his sharpest worry is for senior colleagues like Rosa.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most because neither he nor Ama would have time to finish their training.
whatWouldHelp: Money that keeps people afloat while things settle, protection so trainees aren't the first dropped, and a promise that robots on a public network serve the public.
